exemplar: The passage argues that the Columbian Exchange was a two-way transfer with radically unequal consequences: Europe and Africa gained foods and wealth that fueled population growth, while Native peoples suffered demographic catastrophe from disease and exploitation.

The introduction of Old World crops and animals transformed Native life: horses revolutionized Plains cultures' hunting and warfare, while wheat and cattle reshaped landscapes and diets across the Americas.
The exchange enriched Europe enormously - American silver flowed into Spanish coffers and global trade networks - funding the very empires that were conquering the Americas.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about the consequences of the Columbian Exchange.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific plant or animal transferred in the Columbian Exchange affected life in the Americas.
C. Briefly explain how the Columbian Exchange affected Europe.

stimulus.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
stimulus.text: Historians describe the Columbian Exchange as the most consequential biological event in human history. Contact after 1492 set off a vast two-way transfer of plants, animals, diseases, and peoples between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Europe and Africa gained maize, potatoes, and tomatoes - crops that would fuel population growth for centuries. But for Native peoples of the Americas, the exchange was catastrophic: Old World diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza swept through populations with no immunity, killing a huge proportion of Indigenous Americans within a generation and clearing the way for European conquest and enslavement.

exemplar: Debs argues that wars are class conflicts in disguise: wealthy elites who declare wars never fight them, while working-class people are conscripted to kill and die for interests that are not their own.
Debs was prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917 for this speech and sentenced to ten years in prison - the federal government's most prominent wartime suppression of antiwar dissent.

The Supreme Court upheld Debs's conviction in Debs v. United States (1919), applying the 'clear and present danger' test it had just announced in Schenck v. United States to punish antiwar speech during wartime.
parts: A. Briefly describe Debs's argument about war in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the federal government responded to antiwar dissent like Debs's during World War I.
C. Briefly explain ONE Supreme Court decision that addressed wartime restrictions on speech.

stimulus.attribution: Eugene V. Debs, speech at Canton, Ohio, June 16, 1918.
stimulus.text: The master class has always declared the wars; the subject class has always fought the battles. The master class has had all to gain and nothing to lose, while the subject class has had nothing to gain and all to lose - especially their lives.

stimulus.attribution: Described from 'Map of the Louisiana Purchase Territory,' U.S. National Archives and Records Administration.
stimulus.text: The map shows the Louisiana Purchase territory (shaded) ceded by France to the United States by the treaty of April 30, 1803, stretching from the Mississippi River west to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico north to British Canada. The existing United States lies east of the Mississippi, with Spanish territory to the west and southwest.

parts: A. Briefly explain what the map shows about the territorial growth of the United States by 1803.
B. Briefly explain how the map illustrates the significance of the Louisiana Purchase.
C. Briefly explain one political controversy caused by the territorial acquisition shown on the map.
exemplar: The map shows the Purchase roughly doubling the nation's area, adding a vast territory west of the Mississippi between the existing states and Spanish lands.
The shaded Purchase dwarfs the original states, showing how one treaty instantly made the United States a continental-scale power controlling the Mississippi River's western bank.
The acquisition revived the debate over whether slavery would expand into the new territory, a controversy that produced the Missouri Compromise of 1820.
